tagline: A former livestock route crosses Exeter’s wooded hills and stream valleys.
intro: Route 102 crosses Exeter’s rolling hills and narrow valleys for 7.3 miles between Routes 2 and 3. Designated a Rhode Island scenic roadway in September 1993, it passes hills reaching 560 feet and five valleys containing headwater streams of the Queen’s River watershed. RIDOT highlights the contrast between hilltop panoramas and enclosed valley views, with pine stands and red maples in the wetlands.

Most of the highway follows eighteenth-century Ten Rod Road, which carried goods and livestock to market at the colonial port of Wickford. Significant stretches of its original stone walls remain beside the road.

Heading west from Route 2 toward Route 3 reverses the landscape’s eastward transition from forest to agricultural open space. Ten Rod Road crosses the Queen River, and Lawton’s Mill preserves a wood-frame mill building and surviving waterways along the road. In autumn, the valley and wetland red maples turn scarlet.
notice: Original stone walls remain beside significant stretches of the old Ten Rod Road.

moments.title: Queen River
moments.text: Ten Rod Road crosses the Queen River in Exeter, part of a landscape threaded with headwater streams. The river rises in Dead Swamp in West Greenwich and flows south through Exeter into South Kingstown. There it meets Glen Rock Brook and becomes the Usquepaug River. Sodom Brook, Locke Brook and Rake Factory Brook are among the tributaries feeding it.

moments.title: Chestnut Hill
moments.text: Chestnut Hill Baptist Church is an 1838 Greek Revival building in Exeter. It entered the National Register of Historic Places in 1978.

moments.title: Lawton’s Mill
moments.text: A dam and raceway extend several hundred feet north of Lawton’s Mill on Ten Rod Road. These waterways survive from the mill’s working years, alongside a wood-frame mill building constructed circa 1820. Also called Albro Mill, the property includes an eighteenth-century house and a nineteenth-century barn enlarged in the early twentieth century. The mill entered the National Register of Historic Places in 1980.
